name: Jade Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the crew that repairs overhead lines for the electricity company on the east side of town. My two-year diploma helps with faults that cross circuits, though the thing I insist on is a second test before anyone touches a conductor. I like being trusted with the difficult repairs and I dislike changes announced without a field trial. My partner Sam and I have two children at school, a mortgage, good pay for this job and about nine months of expenses saved. I have never used an AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew to keep checking the isolation and let the office tidy its forms. A shorter report is fine if it leaves the test result exactly where we can find it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our pay and nine-month reserve make a minor office change a small matter at home. I do not like the idea of a generated sentence drifting into the safety section, even if no jobs change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current repair rota and require the meter reading on every signed work sheet. In the first year I would compare the new form with three old fault reports before approving it for my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of annoyance at paperwork. The mortgage is not hanging on a shorter form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you reject the new form?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I could not find the isolation time and meter value in one glance, I would send it back. A lineworker wearing gloves should not hunt through a paragraph for a meter reading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI tool to check it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used one, and a few old reports plus the original readings are enough for this small decision.

say: **Physical isolation** checks remain the basis for safe repair.
**Shorter reports** are acceptable only with visible meter results.
think: Our **nine-month reserve** protects the household in this mild picture.
Generated **safety text** could still be put in the wrong place.
do: **Keep** the current line repair rota and meter checks.
**Compare** the proposed form with three old fault reports before approving it.
S0.quote: A lineworker wearing gloves should not hunt through a paragraph for a meter reading.
fieldNote: Her **high pay and reserve** make the plateau financially secure.
She has **never used AI** and evaluates the form by field usability, not a software demonstration.

steps.text: Keep line repair rota and signed meter checks
Compare new form with three old fault reports

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell dispatch not to shorten a repair slot until a crew has driven the route and isolated the line. Software may take the calls and buying first; our hands still make the repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If office staffing falls, more incomplete jobs could arrive on my truck. That might mean longer shifts rather than lost pay for me, and nearby utilities are hiring, but I want to see a real trial before trusting the new targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have the crew record access and isolation time on six jobs and show the log to our supervisor. During the first year I would ask for a joint field trial with dispatch, then keep the current rota unless the trial shows a workable change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about being handed a schedule that looks right only on a screen. I do not expect my pay to vanish because the call desk changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the log reveal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The road behind the substation has a turn too sharp for our truck. I would mark the detour and the extra isolation time beside the software estimate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you seek another employer now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. There are several nearby utilities, but I would not leave a well-paid line crew over a repair target that has not even been tried.

say: **Desk work** changes first, while a lineworker still tests and repairs the damaged power line.
**Crew trials** should set realistic repair slots.
think: Incomplete **work orders** may lengthen shifts more than cut my wage.
Nearby **utilities** offer choices if this employer eventually gets it wrong.
do: **Log** access and isolation time on six jobs.
**Request** a joint field trial with dispatch and keep the current rota meanwhile.
feel: **Uneasy** about screen-based targets, but financially secure for now.
S1.quote: I would not leave a well-paid line crew over a repair target that has not even been tried.
fieldNote: She treats **field trials** as a test of workability before changing a sound job.
Her **income risk** remains limited in this scenario, though longer shifts would strain the household.

steps.text: Keep current repair rota while six jobs are measured
Request joint dispatch and crew field trial of repair targets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI could take planning and calls by 2028, but full field robots come about 2031. Until then we need the people who can test, climb and put a line back safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot able to do the whole repair could cut my hours after 2031, even with my lead experience. Our nine months of savings and several nearby utilities give us room, but no employer promises another job at my current lineworker wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask payroll for my base pay without callouts and compare it with our mortgage and school costs. In the first year after 2028 I would visit two nearby utilities about senior repair openings; if field robots reduce my hours after 2031, I would apply for the best actual vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing a wage I have worked hard to reach. I am not panicking; there is time and there are places to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam about the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner Sam we can keep school plans for now because we have savings. I would also say we should not count on callout pay to last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a new course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a guess. I would first ask the utilities what work they actually need and whether they would pay for any required training.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes planning before capable repair robots arrive around 2031.
**Human crews** remain needed in the physical-work gap.
think: Field robots may cut my **hours and pay** after 2031.
Nine months saved and **nearby utilities** help, but cannot guarantee equal pay.
do: **Compare** base pay with mortgage and school costs.
**Visit** two nearby utilities after 2028 and apply if field hours shrink after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about wage loss, with a workable search path.
S2.quote: Our nine months of savings and several nearby utilities give us room, but no employer promises another job at my current lineworker wage.
fieldNote: She uses **nine months** as search time, without treating existing savings as a new saving action.
Her **job application** depends on a genuine vacancy and fewer field hours, while training remains only an enquiry.

steps.text: Visit two nearby utilities and apply if field hours shrink after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let the company show what the machines really do before thinking AI arrives in 2031. Field robots follow around 2034, so I would ask for more than a clean-floor demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn a different safety post if it used my repair judgement. But I would not give up high lineworker pay for a title that sounds safe and pays less than our mortgage and school costs require.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would inspect a field robot trial with my crew and ask for the pay scale of any safety post. If there is a local vacancy with paid hands-on training and pay that covers our fixed bills, I would take the training before 2031 and apply after 2031; otherwise I would stay on repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but less pressed than in the two-year picture. A real machine and a real wage could change my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the trial to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot should repair an old line with awkward fittings after rain, then leave a test record another crew can check. A polished robot video would not tell me how it repairs an old power line after rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the safety post pays less than field work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the offer with our fixed bills and decide with Sam. A smaller cheque might be possible, but only if the mortgage and children’s costs stayed covered.

say: **Field trials** must show old lines and difficult weather before 2034.
**Safety roles** should have written pay terms.
think: A new **safety post** could fit my skills if it pays household bills.
I will not trade **high pay** for an untested title.
do: **Inspect** a field robot trial and request the safety pay scale.
**Take** paid hands-on training for a real local bill-covering vacancy.
**Apply** after 2031 if trained; otherwise remain on repairs.
feel: **Uneasy**, but open to proven equipment and credible pay.
S3.quote: A polished robot video would not tell me how it repairs an old power line after rain.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** is tied to proof on old hardware, not a refusal to consider any change.
Her **training and move** require a local opening, paid practice and a bill-covering wage.

steps.text: Observe field robot trial on old lines before deciding
Take paid safety training if local bill-covering vacancy exists
Apply for local safety post after 2031 if trained

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives us time to put rules around field robots before they arrive around 2039. Thinking AI in 2036 might change the paperwork first, but a repair crew will still need a safe line to work on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three I may still have a mortgage balance, and I do not know whether we will want to stop work. With our savings and the local job market, I could wait for a proper offer instead of jumping at the first new title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the line crew role and review our mortgage and savings with Sam each year. In the first year after 2036 I would look at senior inspection vacancies nearby, applying only for a role with pay that covers our bills; I would ask our safety committee to insist on a human stop switch during robot trials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about the time, still alert to the last years of my working pay. I would rather decide whether to leave line repair from a payslip than a robot prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the stop switch need to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A worker standing at the line must be able to halt the robot immediately and log the fault. No manager should have to approve the stop first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you bring retirement forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on this information. Sam and I would review our actual mortgage balance and savings before we discuss any date.

say: **Human stop controls** belong in robot trials before 2039.
**2036 paperwork change** comes before capable robots can do physical field repairs around 2039.
think: I may still owe on the **mortgage** at fifty-three.
Our **savings and local jobs** let us wait for a credible offer.
do: **Keep** leading line repairs and review mortgage finances annually.
**Apply** for nearby senior inspection after 2036 only if pay covers bills.
**Ask** the safety committee to require an immediate worker stop switch.
feel: **Calm** about the runway, alert to future earnings.
S4.quote: I would rather decide whether to leave line repair from a payslip than a robot prediction.
fieldNote: She does not equate a long runway with **early retirement**.
Her **job move** depends on actual pay, while the safety request gives workers direct stopping power.

steps.text: Keep leading repairs and review mortgage with Sam annually
Apply for nearby senior inspection after 2036 only if pay covers bills
Ask safety committee for immediate worker stop switch

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because the field robots arrive around 2031 before I could see a long trial and a settled job market. Written pay and a genuine senior vacancy nearby would help me decide whether to move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether my crew trusts a machine report. I would insist a person at the line can stop a field robot even when its report says the repair is finished.

portrait: **Jade Farah**, 43, leads an electricity line crew and holds a two-year technical diploma.
She lives with partner Sam and **two school-age children**, with a mortgage, high lineworker pay and about nine months saved.
She has **never used AI** and demands meter results, field trials and written pay before accepting new procedures or work.
In **Steady Disruption**, she expects longer shifts more readily than lost wages and measures six repair jobs before changing targets.
The **2028 scenario** raises income risk after 2031, though savings and many nearby utilities give her options.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because field robots could reduce well-paid repair hours around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Written **senior vacancy pay** at a nearby utility would make a possible move concrete.
A worker-controlled **stop switch** would protect crews during robot trials.
headlineQuote: I would insist a person at the line can stop a field robot even when its report says the repair is finished.
